item.title: Achieving the limits of automorphism gates
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — For stabilizer codes encoding k≥3 logical qubits, largest logical group achievable via automorphisms is generated by all addressable S and CX gates, requiring n=Θ(2k) physical qubits (n=2k−1 exactly). By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates require only n=k(k+1)/2=Θ(k2) physical qubits via physical single-qubit Cliffords alone.

Grade 0.504 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Jin Ming Koh, Shayan Majidy, Aranya Chakraborty, Anqi Gong, Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Norman Y. Yao

Figure

Gate group size as a function of the number of logical qubits k across different gate implementations. Solid curves show automorphism, transversal, and permutation gate limits, while dotted lines show diagonal gate groups up to level t of the Clifford hierarchy.

Asks

What is the maximum logical gate group achievable by automorphism gates on stabilizer codes, and what is the minimum physical-qubit cost needed to realize it?

But

Restricted to stabilizer codes (with refinements for CSS and self-dual CSS codes); physical operations limited to single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations (extended to single-qubit diagonal gates for higher hierarchy levels).

Tools

stabilizer code theory · symplectic group and Clifford group classification · complete-hypergraph codes · concatenated non-CSS codes

Abstract

Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing combines versatile but expensive operations with specialized but cheap ones. Its efficiency depends on how much computation can be pushed onto the cheap operations and on the size of the code needed to do so. Automorphism gates provide such cheap operations using only physical single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations. Yet no general theory characterizes their maximum logical power or the minimum code size needed to attain it. We develop such a theory. For stabilizer codes encoding k≥3 logical qubits, we show that the largest logical group attainable by automorphisms is generated by all addressable S and CX gates, and we construct codes attaining it. While this group contains exponentially fewer gates than the full Clifford group, adding one suitable non-Clifford gate yields universality. We further classify the largest logical groups attainable using qubit permutations, physical single-qubit Cliffords, or both across general stabilizer and CSS codes, and derive refined bounds for self-dual CSS subclasses. Achieving the maximum-size logical group through automorphisms requires n=Θ(2^k) physical qubits. By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates, generated by S and CZ, require only n=Θ(k²) physical qubits when implemented using physical single-qubit Cliffords alone. Both bounds are tight. This polynomial qubit cost extends beyond Cliffords to all addressable diagonal gates at any fixed level of the Clifford hierarchy, using physical single-qubit diagonal gates. Thus, for full addressability, the sharpest physical-qubit cost divide lies between diagonal and CX-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates.

item.title: QECirc: A Community-Driven, FAIR Library of Quantum Error Correction Circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Created QECirc (qecirc.com), an open, verified library providing standardized Stim and OpenQASM implementations for quantum error correction circuits spanning encoders, state preparation, and logical gates.

Grade 0.499 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Ludwig Schmid, Tom Peham, Robert Wille

Asks

How can quantum error correction circuits scattered across papers and ad-hoc repositories be standardized, verified, and made interoperable?

Before

Error Correction Zoo catalogs QEC code properties, but lacks concrete, format-agnostic implementation circuits.

But

Syndrome-extraction schedules and larger qLDPC code families such as bivariate-bicycle codes remain planned work.

Tools

QECirc · Stim · OpenQASM · Crumble · Quirk

Abstract

Quantum error correction (QEC) underpins fault-tolerant quantum computing, but the circuits that realize QEC codes (encoders, logical state-preparation and gate routines, and syndrome-extraction schedules) are scattered across papers and one-off repositories in incompatible formats, often documented too sparsely to reconstruct or reuse. We present QECirc (https://qecirc.com/), a community-driven, open library that makes QEC circuits Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). Each entry links to its underlying code, ships in Stim and OpenQASM with interactive visualizations, and is checked for correctness before publication. In short, where a catalog such as the Error Correction Zoo describes the codes, QECirc provides the concrete circuits that realize them.

item.title: Scalable logical qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Defines scalable logical qubits and establishes a benchmark framework across four dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance.

Grade 0.485 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Matthias Troyer, Chetan Nayak, John Martinis

Asks

How to define and measure meaningful progress toward fault-tolerant logical qubits capable of supporting utility-scale algorithms.

But

Conceptual framework and metrics definition; no empirical performance data presented.

Tools

quantum error correction · real-time decoding and feedback · fault-tolerant universal gate architectures

Abstract

Utility-scale quantum computing will require executing long, complex algorithms with end-to-end error rates far below what physical qubits can support directly. Error-corrected logical qubits are needed to achieve this goal. To make the progress on logical qubits measurable and comparable we introduce the definition of scalable logical qubits: logical qubits preserved for long computations by repeated quantum error correction, capable of fault-tolerant universal operations with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, and replicable to the hundreds or thousands, as required by applications. We characterize these scalable logical qubits along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance, and discuss trade-offs among these dimensions.

item.title: Coherent error threshold for quantum LDPC codes
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Proves general stabilizer qLDPC codes with distance dn=Ω(log⁡n) have nonzero code capacity thresholds under local coherent noise, with logical diamond-distance error decaying as supU⁡εn⋆(U,η)≤Cne−cdn for optimal recovery and supU⁡εnMW(U,η)≤2nχMW(1−ρMW)ρMWdn under minimum-weight decoding.

Grade 0.465 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes” · Zhengyi Han, Yuanchen Zhao, Yijia Xu, Yixu Wang, Zi-Wen Liu

Figure

Schematic of the cluster resummation technique, showing how differentiating with respect to the interpolation parameter t marks a single connected large component while resumming all disconnected error configurations.

Asks

Do general quantum LDPC codes admit rigorous nonzero error correction thresholds under coherent and general local noise?

Before

Rigorous fault tolerance under coherent noise had been established for constant-rate qLDPC codes with linear distance d=Θ(n) (Fawzi et al. 2024), but not for sublinear distance codes such as topological or quantum expander codes.

But

Applies to code capacity model: noiseless syndrome measurements and recovery circuits following depth-D, bounded-support (r) local coherent or local CPTP noise.

Tools

cluster resummation · approximate quantum error correction (AQEC) · diamond norm bounds on complementary channels · minimum-weight decoding analysis

Abstract

A key appeal of quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes is their ability to suppress stochastic Pauli noise below nonzero thresholds. Coherent errors are fundamentally different: they produce superpositions of error patterns whose amplitudes can interfere even after syndrome measurement. Rigorous understanding of coherent errors remains limited. Here we show that general qLDPC codes admit a nonzero code capacity threshold against local coherent noise and more generally local channel noise. For any family of qLDPC codes with distance d=Ω(logn), we show that there is a constant noise strength below which the logical recovery error in diamond distance decays exponentially with the code distance. The result is established for optimal recovery as well as the minimum-weight decoder. The key technical ingredient is what we call a emphcluster resummation: rather than bounding superposed error configurations one by one, we isolate a large connected error cluster in the channel expansion and exactly resum all errors disconnected from it before taking norms. Standard cluster counting then yields exponential suppression. This work resolves a longstanding challenge in fault tolerance theory, providing general robustness guarantees for qLDPC codes against coherent noise and laying a rigorous foundation for future studies of fault-tolerant quantum technologies.

item.title: Fast Unitary Preparation of Surface-Code Logical States on Neutral-Atom Hardware
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Bidirectional middle-out CNOT cascade prepares surface-code logical states in depth (d+3)/2 with fault distance d in the protected error direction, requiring ≈34(d+3) collective AOD shuttles and ≈14(d+3) row pickups.

Grade 0.454 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille

Figure

Logical error rate versus noise scaling factor across code distances 3, 7, and 11. Bidirectional cascade remains sub-threshold at scaling factor 1 for both logical states, outperforming unidirectional and single-pivot methods.

Asks

How can unitary stabilizer-expanding surface-code state preparation be adapted to minimize depth and shuttling constraints on neutral-atom processors?

Before

Unitary single-pivot preparation was 3(d−1) CZ layers and 4(d−1) shuttles; unidirectional cascade was d CZ layers and ≈32d shuttles.

But

Fault-tolerant only in protected direction (conjugate direction allows weight-2 errors requiring an intermediate QEC round). Circuit-level numerical simulation up to 107 shots under calibrated device noise, not physical hardware measurement.

Tools

Acousto-optic-deflector (AOD) shuttling · Global Rydberg CZ gates · Bloqade toolchain · Stim · PyMatching

Code. https://github.com/lsschmid/fast-surface-code

Abstract

Preparing logical states is a constantly recurring primitive at the start of any surface-code-based quantum computation. The standard measurement-based protocol is expensive on neutral atoms, since measurements are orders of magnitude slower than gates and, on single-zone architectures, additionally require shuttling the atoms to a readout zone. In this work, we present a measurement-free, unitary preparation of surface-code Pauli eigenstates tailored to neutral atoms. A bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade grows the patch from its middle line outward in depth (d+3)/2, while retaining fault distance d in the protected error direction. Each layer maps to one collective atom move followed by a single global Rydberg pulse, with about one row pickup per two layers. We compile and simulate the resulting schedules with the open-source bloqade toolchain under a hardware-calibrated, circuit-level neutral-atom noise model. The bidirectional cascade achieves the lowest logical error rate at every distance, and is the only construction tested that operates below threshold for both logical states at the considered device-level noise.

item.title: Scalable entanglement distribution using encoded hybrid repeater chains
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Hybrid quantum repeater chains combining fast, multiplexable type-1 memories with long-coherence type-2 memories achieve higher end-to-end entanglement distribution rates than pure architectures of either platform alone, even when inter-platform gate errors are non-zero.

Grade 0.452 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Stav Haldar, Saikat Guha, Don Towsley, Filip Rozpkedek

Figure

Entanglement distribution rate and end-to-end fidelity plotted against total chain distance L at l0=20 km spacing. Encoded hybrid architectures maintain non-zero distribution rates out to thousands of kilometers, outperforming pure type-1 and type-2 setups.

Asks

How should heterogeneous quantum memory platforms and quantum error-correction capabilities be allocated along a repeater chain to maximize entanglement distribution rates under realistic hardware constraints?

But

Circuit-level noise model simulations; fixed inter-node spacing of l0=20 km; independent logical error channels after physical combinatorial counting.

Tools

Monte Carlo circuit-level noise simulations · Fault-tolerant stabilizer measurement via GHZ ancillae · Modified swap-as-soon-as-possible (swap-ASAP) policy · Three-qubit repetition, Steane [[7,1,3]], and Shor [[9,1,3]] codes

Abstract

Long-distance entanglement distribution requires error correction protocols to compensate for qubit decoherence in quantum memories and noise introduced during entanglement swapping. We argue that repeater chains with error-correction capabilities should exploit more than one physical platform, combining the complementary strengths of different quantum memory technologies into a single hybrid repeater architecture. An important constituent of such an architecture is a hybrid repeater which combines type-1 memories, characterized by fast entanglement generation rates and suitability for multiplexing, and type-2 memories that offer long coherence times and low two-qubit gate error rates. Taking the resource-intensive nature of hybrid nodes into account, we propose and analyze repeater chains in which only a subset of nodes need to be hybrid, while the remaining nodes are simpler first-generation repeaters with no error-correction capability. Through detailed Monte Carlo simulations of fault-tolerant encoded repeater chain protocols based on the three-qubit phase-flip repetition code, the [[7,1,3]] Steane code, and the [[9,1,3]] Shor code, we demonstrate that these hybrid architectures outperform pure architectures based on a single memory platform in terms of end-to-end entanglement distribution rate. In our study we develop a full circuit-level noise model of our architectures and examine the impact of an imperfect interface between the two platforms on our hybrid architecture. We also develop a modified version of the swap-as-soon-as-possible policy with multiplexing, more suited to our architecture where some nodes perform error-correction while others do not. This modified policy significantly reduces the information storage time in memory qubits relative to the previously considered swap policies in encoded repeater chains.

item.title: Quantum computers will not be that different: A blueprint for quantum computer architecture at scale
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Defines modular blueprint for utility-scale quantum systems treating QPUs as classical heterogeneous accelerators with specialized low-level hardware for control, readout, and real-time quantum error correction (QEC).

Grade 0.451 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Torsten Hoefler, Matthias Troyer

Asks

How should utility-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing systems be architected at the system level?

But

Architectural and conceptual framework; dependent on physical layer delivering baseline fault-tolerant physical qubit thresholds.

Tools

Instruction set architecture abstraction · High-performance networking stack models · Hardware-specialized QEC decoders · Heterogeneous accelerator architecture principles

Abstract

Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

item.arxave:question: How should utility-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing systems be architected at the system level?
item.arxave:limits: Architectural and conceptual framework; dependent on physical layer delivering baseline fault-tolerant physical qubit thresholds.
item.arxave:tools: Instruction set architecture abstraction · High-performance networking stack models · Hardware-specialized QEC decoders · Heterogeneous accelerator architecture principles
item.arxave:abstract: Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

item.title: Blind Quantum Computation with a Small Quantum Server
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructed blind quantum computation (Blind PBC) requiring a quantum server of only t qubits for an n-qubit circuit with t non-Clifford T gates, achieving perfect information-theoretic input secrecy with four-way random state preparation and a single t-qubit quantum communication step.

Grade 0.433 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Daniel Lovsted, Filipa C. R. Peres, Joshua Nevin, Selman Ipek, Anne Broadbent

Figure

Comparison of standard Pauli-based computation (a) with Blind PBC (b), illustrating state preparation with client random phase rotations SciZdi, adaptive Pauli observable measurement via client-side circuit modification 𝖯𝖡𝖢.𝖲𝖾𝗅(C𝐱∗), and output sample decoding.

Asks

How can blind quantum computation be performed while minimizing the required quantum processor size on the server?

Before

Server size was n+t qubits for single-instance communication or n+1 qubits with t sequential communication rounds in quantum computing on encrypted data (QCED).

But

Hides computational basis input 𝐱 (or orthonormal stabilizer bases) but reveals circuit structure C. Qubit virtualization incurs classical sampling cost exponential in simulated virtual qubit count k.

Tools

Pauli-based computation (PBC) · Magic state teleportation gadgets · One-way four-phase quantum state encryption · Tailored resource computation (TRC)

Abstract

Blind quantum computation (BQC) allows low-resource clients to securely delegate computations to a quantum server, but server resource costs scale with the computation size, posing a bottleneck for implementations. By leveraging Pauli-based computation (PBC), we achieve BQC with a server whose size depends only on the non-Clifford gate count. Our protocol inherits fault tolerance and qubit virtualization from PBC and reveals that classical-client BQC is possible even in the absence of classical simulability. Finally, we present an entanglement-based dual protocol that performs a resource state computation with a dramatically reduced execution cost.
